question: Given the rain of the whole local day t (00:00 to 24:00 by the local wall clock, from hourly AORC rain: 1 km, anchored on gauges and radar, the mean over the basin outline) as one extra daily input, how many more onsets are warned 1 day ahead, and how much of the gap to the perfect weather forecast is closed - against the same AORC rain over the rain table's own window (no new hour), against the rain table alone, against the ERA5 rain to midnight of experiment E1 and against NLDAS rain whose day ends in the evening? And does a rain table with the right clock (the Daymet rain column replaced by that AORC rain, no extra column) beat the mis-stamped Daymet table on its own?
outcome: Given the rain of the whole issue day up to local midnight (hourly AORC rain, 1 km, from 00:00 to 24:00 by the local wall clock) as one extra input to the LSTM with the river gauge, onsets warned 1 day ahead go from 19% with the rain table alone to 52% (single trainings 49% to 55%; the onsets of one storm are not independent): +33.1 points over the rain table alone and +33.7 points over the control with the same AORC rain over the table's own window (18%); the median NSE goes from 0.59 to 0.76 (the seed-averaged forecast; single trainings 0.68 to 0.77); the verdict of results/flood_analysis.json is NOT YET for the onsets and CAUTION for all high-flow days.
outcome_caveat: The ERA5 rain to midnight of script 15 gives a lower share (29%, 180 hits of 611) than the AORC rain to midnight (52%, 316 hits of 611); the NLDAS rain up to the evening gives a lower share (30%, 183 hits of 611) than the AORC rain to midnight (52%, 316 hits of 611); the five single trainings with the AORC rain to midnight span 48.6% to 55.3%; the success rule of the work order (clearly above the NLDAS result in every training, control flat) is met. The control with the same AORC rain over the table's own window is flat (18.0% against 18.7% with the rain table alone), so the gain of 33.7 points over that control (33.1 points over the rain table alone) comes from the hours after about 09:00 (228 onsets warned only by the AORC rain to midnight against 22 only by that control). Against the ERA5 rain to midnight over the same hours the AORC rain warns of +22.3 points (316 against 180 hits of 611; every training with AORC above every training with ERA5: yes), so the E1 gain grows with it (step 1b of the roadmap). Ridge regression and the random forest given the same input warn of 55.2% and 48.0% (the new input adds 44.5 and 29.8 points to them, 33.1 to the LSTM), so the gain does not need the network. On the median NSE the LSTM (0.76) against ridge regression (0.64) and the random forest (0.66): report section 4.2 reads 'the LSTM is ahead' for ridge regression and 'the LSTM is ahead' for the forest; on the onsets, the headline, ridge regression warns of more (55.2% against 51.7%, 67% of its warnings false against 51%; 1 of the 5 LSTM trainings is above it); the random forest warns of fewer (48.0% against 51.7%, 53% of its warnings false against 51%; 5 of the 5 LSTM trainings are above it). With the AORC rain in the place of the Daymet rain column (no extra column) the LSTM warns of 53% of the onsets against 19% with the Daymet rain table (44.8% to 54.8% against 18.0% to 18.5% in the single trainings; +33.9 points over the rain table alone, more in every training), but that comparison changes the product (Daymet to AORC) and the clock (a day that ends at about 09:00 to one that ends at midnight) together and is not a verdict on the Daymet product: the same AORC rain over the table's own window adds -0.7 points to the rain table alone, over the whole day it adds +33.7 points to that control, the replaced table adds +33.9 points to the rain table alone, and against AORC as an extra column it adds +0.8 points (no clear difference); the data support that the hours after about 09:00 are worth about 34 points (the two gains above, averaged), and whether the Daymet product itself costs skill apart from its clock was not isolated (AORC over 09:00 to 09:00 in the place of the Daymet column was not run). AORC is a retrospective analysis, not rain that could be read at midnight: its hours are daily totals on a gauge day that ends at 12 UTC, spread over the hours with radar and corrected about 10 days behind real time, and the hours before 2002, which are all the training years, are disaggregated daily totals. An independent review (results/review_aorc_rain_to_midnight.json) tested what that could do to the test years: on 78 days (936 basin-days) the AORC rain before local midnight does not depend on the Stage IV rain after it (coefficient -0.030 mm per mm, 95% interval -0.060 to -0.001), and with Stage IV, a real-time product (about one hour behind), in place of AORC on the issue day the three networks of seeds 0-2 that the review tested warn of 86 to 95 of the 171 onsets of those days against 92 with AORC (the rain table alone: 15), that is 92% to 104% of the AORC effect; a hindsight that the review could not exclude would cost those networks at most about 3 points of their 51% (16 of 313 hits); the other 440 onsets were not tested by the review; with all five networks, Stage IV in place of AORC on the issue day costs 22 of 316 hits on all 611 onsets (3.6 points; 5 hits, 0.8 points, with the level of AORC restored). Stage IV in place of AORC on the issue day of all 611 onsets (results/stage4_realtime.json): 294 of 611 warned against 316 with AORC and 114 with the rain table alone, 89% of the AORC effect survives (95% interval 83% to 95%, drawing issue days); with the last hour of the issue day taken out, as the delay of Stage IV would, 276 are warned (80% of the effect) and with the level of AORC restored (Stage IV times 1.06) 311. That count is driven by heavy rain on the issue day more than by its exact amount: with the Stage IV rain of another onset day of the same basin in its place 286 onsets are warned, with the AORC rain of an ordinary day 36, with no rain 13; the mean absolute error of the forecast on the onset days, which does depend on the exact rain, is 4.64 mm/day with Stage IV, 4.62 with AORC and 5.64 with another onset's rain.

inputs.how_to_read: the hours each input covers, as the model reads them on issue day t. The forecast is issued at the end of day t, local midnight of the river-flow day

clock.input: prcp (Daymet rain, the rain table), srad, tmax, tmin, vp, dayl
clock.used_by: every set (in wqa_rep the rain column prcp is replaced by aorc_to_midnight)
clock.covers: for rain, a day that ends at about 09:00 local standard time on day t (basins 07:26 to 18:16; the four readings 07:28 to 10:42); the window of the other Daymet variables was not measured

clock.input: q_mm (observed river flow, with-gauge sets only)
clock.used_by: every set of this script, wq, wqn, wqh, wqnh, wqf and their controls
clock.covers: the daily mean flow of local day t, midnight to midnight by the local clock, so the day ends at the issue time (in the 2012 check, while summer time was in force, by the summer clock at 10 of 12 gauges and by standard time at 2; by standard time in winter)

clock.used_by: wqa (an extra column), wqa_rep (in the place of the Daymet rain)
clock.covers: AORC hourly rain (the mean of the 1 km cells inside the basin outline, data/aorc) of the local wall-clock day t, summer time included: every hour goes to the local calendar day in which it ends, so the last hour of day t ends at 24:00 by the wall clock, the end of day t and the issue time; a day has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change; time zones: America/Chicago for Leaf River, MS (UTC-6 in winter); America/New_York for all other basins (UTC-5 in winter)

clock.input: aorc_to_09 (new: the control with no new hour)

AORC hourly rain of the UTC day of the date of day t: from 00:00 UTC of that date to 00:00 UTC of the next date, always 24 hours (the day that a rain product served by UTC day holds, as IMERG at NASA POWER); in local standard time it ends at 19:00 in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Central time, by the wall clock between 18:00 and 20:00 (summer time), 4 to 6 hours before the issue time (local midnight at the end of day t)

aorc_data.what: NOAA AORC v1.1 hourly rain (APCP_surface) reduced to one hourly basin-mean series per study basin, for experiment E1b (code/16_aorc_rain_to_midnight.py)
aorc_data.mask_how: the cells whose centre lies inside the basin outline (CAMELS HCDN_nhru_final_671.shp), cells of the nominal 1/120 degree grid, rasterio.features.rasterize with all_touched=False; the basin mean is the plain mean of those cells: the cell area varies by less than 1% over the largest basin (cell_area_variation_over_the_basin), so area weights would change nothing worth keeping

stored_coordinates.note: the coordinate arrays are written with a rounded step (0.008333 instead of 1/120 = 0.0083333...), so they drift from the nominal grid by up to the amount above; the grid is taken as the nominal 1/120 degree grid (ilat = round((lat - 20) * 120), ilon = round((lon + 130) * 120)); the stored arrays would shift the cells of a basin by a fraction of one cell at most

grid.index_formula: ilat = round((lat - 20) * 120), ilon = round((lon + 130) * 120); the latitude axis ascends (index 0 = 20.0 N)

time_stamps.convention: UTC; every yearly store starts at 00:00 on 1 January and the stamps of consecutive stores follow each other hour by hour (asserted for every year and over the whole span); the metadata call the stamp 'verification time generated by wgrib2 function verftime()' and do not say whether it is the start or the end of the hour. Evidence on that, in order of sharpness: (1) stamp_check_against_stage_iv (this download): the stamp against the hourly Stage IV files (a file labelled T holds the hour that ends at T) of storm days of the test years, of 2003-2004 and of 2000-2001; (2) results/data_access.json: r = 0.991 against Stage IV at lag 0 and 0.53 at lag +-1 on 2014-01-02 (a scouting measurement of one day); (3) summary.best_hourly_lag_against_era5_by_basin and per_basin.hourly_against_era5_by_lag: the lag profile against the cached ERA5 hourly rain (the hour ending at the stamp), before 2002 and from 2002

test_years.what: correlation of the hourly AORC basin means (stamp T) with the hourly Stage IV basin means (the file labelled T: the hour ending at T) at lags k of -3 to +3 hours (AORC at T against Stage IV at T-k), pooled over the 12 basins and the storm days; k = 0 is the stamp as the END of the hour, k = -1 the stamp as the START of the hour

years_2003_2004.what: correlation of the hourly AORC basin means (stamp T) with the hourly Stage IV basin means (the file labelled T: the hour ending at T) at lags k of -3 to +3 hours (AORC at T against Stage IV at T-k), pooled over the 12 basins and the storm days; k = 0 is the stamp as the END of the hour, k = -1 the stamp as the START of the hour

years_2000_2001.what: correlation of the hourly AORC basin means (stamp T) with the hourly Stage IV basin means (the file labelled T: the hour ending at T) at lags k of -3 to +3 hours (AORC at T against Stage IV at T-k), pooled over the 12 basins and the storm days; k = 0 is the stamp as the END of the hour, k = -1 the stamp as the START of the hour

questions: Does the E1 gain hold or grow when the rain to midnight comes from AORC (gauge- and radar-anchored, 1 km, basin mean) instead of ERA5? (wqa, against wqh and wqn)
What are the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t worth, apart from having a second rain product? (wqa_to09: the same AORC hours over the window of the rain table)
What are the evening hours beyond the UTC day worth? (wqa_utc: the same AORC hours over the UTC day, what a rain product served by UTC day or IMERG-Early would hold at the issue time)
Does a rain table with the right clock beat the mis-stamped table on its own? (wqa_rep = wqa_daymet_replaced: the Daymet rain column replaced by the AORC rain of the wall-clock day t)
Would ridge regression and a random forest gain from the new input as the LSTM does? (the yardstick, rule 2 of the work order)

aorc_utc_day.description: AORC hourly rain of the UTC day of the date of day t: from 00:00 UTC of that date to 00:00 UTC of the next date, always 24 hours (the day that a rain product served by UTC day holds, as IMERG at NASA POWER); in local standard time it ends at 19:00 in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Central time, by the wall clock between 18:00 and 20:00 (summer time), 4 to 6 hours before the issue time (local midnight at the end of day t)

check_windows.how_to_read: correlation of the Daymet rain (daymet) and of the NLDAS rain (nldas) stamped day d with the AORC series of the same name of day d-1 (day_before), d (same_day) and d+1 (day_after)

roadmap_step_1b.rule: success is that the E1 gain holds or grows. value_of_hours_09_to_24.what: the worth of the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t, with the river gauge: lstm_wqa (AORC rain from 00:00 to 24:00 of day t) minus lstm_wqa_to09 (the same AORC hours over the window of the rain table itself, 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t: a second rain product that holds no hour the table does not cover, as far as the table's window is known). The two differ only in the extra column; the same seed number gives the same starting weights and the same sequence of training samples (difference_by_seed). ITS COMPANION is second_rain_product_alone (lstm_wqa_to09 minus lstm_wq: 18.0% against 18.7%, -0.7 points, every seed above every seed: no): the control is flat, so this difference is the worth of the hours after about 09:00 and not that of having a second product. Quote the two together.

value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day.what: the worth of the evening hours beyond the UTC day, with the river gauge: lstm_wqa (00:00 to 24:00 of day t) minus lstm_wqa_utc (the same AORC hours over the UTC day of day t, which ends at 00:00 UTC of day t+1, 19:00 local standard time in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Leaf River): what a rain product served by UTC day, or IMERG-Early with its delay of about 4 hours, would hold at the issue time, so the difference is what the last hours before the issue time add to it (AORC summed over the UTC day stands in for such a product; it is not one). THIS IS A READING OF AORC and is to be quoted together with nldas_rain_against_aorc_over_the_utc_day (and, for ERA5's own value of the same hours, with script 15's value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day): the NLDAS rain, whose day ends at about the hour at which the UTC day ends (17:30 as measured, 19:00 if it is stamped by the UTC day), reaches 30.0% (183 hits), the AORC rain over the UTC day 38.3% (234 hits) and the AORC rain to midnight 51.7% (316 hits). So the +13.4 points are what the evening hours beyond the UTC day add to AORC rain, and a product whose day ends about there stays below the AORC rain to midnight.

value_of_hours_09_to_utc_day_end.what: the hours in between: lstm_wqa_utc minus lstm_wqa_to09, the worth of the hours from about 09:00 to the end of the UTC day (19:00 local standard time) of day t, so that the controls read as a ladder: rain table window -> UTC day -> whole day.

second_rain_product_alone.what: what a second rain product with no new hours is worth: lstm_wqa_to09 minus lstm_wq (the rain table alone). If it is not above the seeds of lstm_wq the control is flat in the sense of the work order.

aorc_against_era5.what: AORC against ERA5 over the same hours, with the river gauge: lstm_wqa minus lstm_wqh (script 15). Both give the rain of the wall-clock day t from 00:00 to 24:00 as one extra daily input; they differ in the product only: ERA5 is model rain at the 0.25 degree grid point of the basin centroid, AORC an analysis anchored on gauges and radar, the mean of the 1 km cells inside the outline (and, in the training years before 2002, with hours that are disaggregated daily totals). So the difference is the worth of the product, not of the hours. Quote it together with aorc_against_nldas: the two product comparisons are read in pairs, ERA5 over the same hours and NLDAS over the evening window.

aorc_against_nldas.what: AORC to midnight against NLDAS rain, with the river gauge: lstm_wqa minus lstm_wqn (script 10). NLDAS is the gauge-based hourly analysis shipped with CAMELS; its day ends in the evening (about 17:30 local standard time as measured, 19:00 if it is stamped by the UTC day), so the two differ in the product and in the last hours of the day; for two products over about the same window see nldas_rain_against_aorc_over_the_utc_day. Quote it together with aorc_against_era5: the two product comparisons are read in pairs, ERA5 over the same hours and NLDAS over the evening window.

nldas_rain_against_aorc_over_the_utc_day.what: two rain products over about the same window: lstm_wqn (the NLDAS rain, whose day ends at about 17:30 local standard time as measured, at 19:00 if it is stamped by the UTC day) minus lstm_wqa_utc (the AORC rain over the UTC day, which ends at 19:00): the NLDAS day is known only to within the spread of the readings in results/day_windows.json, so the difference is mostly that of the product, a gauge-based daily analysis against an analysis made with hourly radar, and not that of the hours.

aorc_against_nldas_and_era5_together.what: AORC to midnight against the two older rain products together: lstm_wqa minus lstm_wqnh (script 15: the NLDAS rain of the issue day and the ERA5 rain to midnight as two extra columns). Does one product with the right clock beat the two together?

rain_table_with_the_right_clock.what: does a rain table with the right clock beat the mis-stamped table on its own? lstm_wqa_rep (= wqa_daymet_replaced: the Daymet rain column replaced by the AORC rain of the wall-clock day t, no extra column, the same number of inputs as lstm_wq) against lstm_wq (the Daymet rain table, whose day ends at about 09:00 local time), and against lstm_wqa (the AORC rain as an extra column beside the Daymet rain). The replaced table holds, day by day, all the hours that the table plus the extra column hold, except that the Daymet product itself is gone: against lstm_wq it is the worth of the right clock together with the change of product; against lstm_wqa it is the worth of keeping the Daymet column as well.

by_period.how_to_read: onsets warned 1 day ahead (seed averages, pooled over the basins) and the median NSE, scored on the target days of the test years before and from 17 July 2009 (flood.evaluate with the test part cut in two). A description made after the fact, not one of the readings and not used for any choice. It belongs to the comparison with ERA5 (aorc_against_era5, and the ERA5 sets of the ladder): ERA5's rain was made without rain observations before that day and with radar and gauge rain assimilated over the USA from it; AORC has no such change within the test years (all of them lie after 2002, the first year whose hours come from radar according to the summary of its methods in results/data_access.json), all training and validation years lie before it, and the two parts hold different numbers of onsets, so a difference between them is weak evidence unless it is large; onsets_warned_standard_error is sqrt(p(1-p)/n) of the share.
by_period.source: Beck et al. 2019, Hydrology and Earth System Sciences 23, 207 (citing Lopez 2011 and 2013); read on 2026-10-07; not found in ECMWF's own documentation page

yardstick.what: Rule 2 of NEXT_STEPS_FOR_AGENTS.md: the new input (wqa: past weather + river gauge + the AORC rain to midnight) is also given to ridge regression and the random forest, built and fitted by the recipe of 02_baselines.py (features.feature_table for wq, plus the same rain features of the new series; one model per basin and lead, fitted on the training years only; the ridge strength and the forest settings are those 02_baselines.py chose on the validation years for the input set wq and are not chosen again; the test years are only scored). The scores of lstm_wqa are read beside them in the way 04_lstm_all.py reads the LSTM against the simple models: the single seeds, the basins won, the Wilcoxon p, and the reading of report section 4.2 (11_key_figure.reading); the simple models of script 15 (the same recipe with the ERA5 rain to midnight) are in table_test, and aorc_against_era5_for_each_model sets each model's AORC result against its ERA5 result.

notes: Quoting. The sentence in `outcome` is accurate arithmetic but incomplete as a statement of the result: any document (report, README, slides, Q&A, guide) must quote `outcome_full` (the outcome plus `outcome_caveat`), never `outcome` alone. Both are computed from the tables of this file. The readings of the controls are quoted in pairs (see the text of each reading).

Clock of aorc_to_midnight (the first new input; the windows of the controls follow in the note on the clock of the controls). The value of day t is the rain of the wall-clock day t at the gauge, summer time included (time zones: America/Chicago for Leaf River, MS (UTC-6 in winter); America/New_York for all other basins (UTC-5 in winter)). Every hourly value goes to the local calendar day in which its hour ENDS, and an hour that ends at exactly 24:00 belongs to the day that ends then. A day has 24 hours, or 23 or 25 where the clocks change: 34 days of 23 hours, 12350 of 24 and 34 of 25 (the same in every basin; daily_rain.day_lengths), and summer time is in force at the end of 58% of the days. The first hour of a day starts at 00:00 and the last ends at 24:00, the end of day t, when the forecast is issued. The code checks it for all 12 basins and all 12418 days (1980-10-01 to 2014-09-30, no gap, asserted), exactly as 15_rain_to_midnight.py does for ERA5: (1) every hour summed into a day starts at or after 00:00 and ends at or before 24:00 of that day, by the wall clock and in absolute (UTC) time; (2) the same daily rain by a second route, in which the UTC start and end of every day come from the time-zone rules (zoneinfo) and the hours between them are summed, and every hour lies in the same day as in the main route; (3) the rain of all hours after 24:00 of 3 random days per basin and of the first day of 23 and of 25 hours was replaced by made-up values: no value up to that day changed (daily_rain.clock).

Hour stamps. Each yearly AORC store gives every hour a time stamp, 'verification time generated by wgrib2 function verftime()', in seconds since 1970-01-01 (results/aorc_data.json: store_layout, time_stamps); this script and code/fetch_aorc.py read the time axis of every store from the store itself and assert that it is hourly, that each store starts at 00:00 on 1 January and that the stamps of one store are followed, one hour later, by those of the next, from 1980 to 2014. That the stamp is the END of the hour is not written in the metadata of the stores; it rests on (a) the wording 'verification time', which for an accumulated field is normally the end of its period (not checked here against the wgrib2 documentation), (b) the measurement of results/data_access.json: the hourly rain at the 12 centroids on 2014-01-02 correlates r = 0.991 with the Stage IV hour-ending files at lag 0 and 0.53 at lags of plus or minus one hour (a measurement of one day, made by the scouting agent, not repeated here), (c) the lag profile of the AORC basin-mean hourly rain against the cached ERA5 hourly rain (the hour ending at its stamp, see script 15), median of the basins: from 2002 on the correlation is 0.42 at lag -1, 0.41 at lag 0 and 0.37 at lag +1 (best lag: lag -1 in 9 basins, lag +0 in 3 basins); before 2002 it is 0.44, 0.41 and 0.37 (best lag: lag -1 in 11 basins, lag +0 in 1 basins) (results/aorc_data.json, per_basin.hourly_against_era5_by_lag; a lag of -1 would mean that the AORC value at stamp T matches the ERA5 value of the hour that ENDS one hour later, as a stamp at the START of the hour would, but it also holds the difference in timing between the two products, which is large before 2002, where AORC's hours are disaggregated daily totals); (d) the stamp against the hourly Stage IV files (a file labelled T holds the hour ending at T; the radar analysis that AORC follows from 2002 on, according to the summary of its methods), the hourly basin means of both: test years: 4 storm days (2009-11-11, 2010-02-05, 2008-12-11, 2013-11-26), pooled correlation 0.725 at lag -1, 0.977 at lag 0 and 0.726 at lag +1, best lag +0 (best lag basin by basin: +0 in 12); 2003-2004: 3 storm days (2004-09-07, 2003-07-02, 2003-11-19), pooled correlation 0.767 at lag -1, 0.959 at lag 0 and 0.764 at lag +1, best lag +0 (best lag basin by basin: +0 in 12); 2000-2001: 3 storm days (2001-03-29, 2001-01-19, 2001-09-14), pooled correlation 0.597 at lag -1, 0.669 at lag 0 and 0.648 at lag +1, best lag +0 (best lag basin by basin: -1 in 2, +0 in 6, +1 in 2, +2 in 1, +3 in 1) (results/aorc_data.json, time_stamps.stamp_check_against_stage_iv). (An oddity that fits the stamps, not an error: the first slot of each yearly store, 00:00 on 1 January, is the hour that ends at 00:00, that is the last hour of the year before.) Reading: in the test years the stamp is the END of the hour, to the resolution of the hourly Stage IV files (best lag +0; the correlation at lag 0 is 0.25 higher than at the better of the two neighbouring lags). Before 2002 the hours are disaggregated daily totals and no hourly radar reference exists for them (the Stage IV files of 2000-2001 do not give a sharp peak: pooled correlation 0.60 at lag -1, 0.67 at lag 0, 0.65 at lag +1), so the convention of those years is inferred from the same lag profile against ERA5 before and after 2002, not shown. The proofs of the clock in this file hold GIVEN that convention. If the values were instead the rain of the hour AFTER their stamp, each daily value would hold the first hour after midnight in place of the first hour of the day (the daily series would change by 0.24 mm on average, correlation 0.994 with the main series): the saved networks of wqa, given the series that results from that convention (stamp_convention_check; a sensitivity, not a retraining), warn of 48.6% of the onsets 1 day ahead instead of 51.7% (-3.1 points; median NSE 0.753 instead of 0.764), against a gain of 33.1 points that the input brings over the rain table alone.

Summer time. One rule for all basins: the day is the wall-clock day of the gauge, summer time included, not the standard-time day. Why: results/day_windows.json (15-minute flow of the gauges, 2012-03-13 to 2012-06-25, while summer time was in force) found that the daily flow of 10 of 12 gauges is a midnight-to-midnight mean by the summer clock (over the whole check, 2012-01-05 to 2012-06-25, standard-time weeks included, the tally is 7 by the summer clock and 5 by standard time), so their river-flow day, and with it the issue time of the forecast, ends at 24:00 by the wall clock, which is 23:00 standard time. For the other 2 gauges (Murder Creek, GA; Turkey Creek, GA) the flow day follows standard time, so the wall-clock day ends one hour before their flow day: for them one hour of rain is left out in summer, which can only lose information and never reads anything after the issue time. In winter the wall clock is standard time. Only 2012-01-05 to 2012-06-25 was checked, so how the flow days of the other years were cut is not known; the rule reads nothing after the issue time whether a gauge's flow day follows the wall clock or standard time. What the hour that is left out for some gauges in summer would be worth was not measured.

What the series is. AORC v1.1 (NOAA, National Weather Service, Office of Water Prediction: 'Analysis Of Record for Calibration') is an hourly analysis on a 1/120 degree (about 1 km) grid, 1979 to 2025, one open Zarr store per year (AWS Open Data). As results/data_access.json records it (from a search summary of the NWS methods read on 2026-10-07; the methods document itself could not be rendered there, so this is a secondary source), the daily precipitation of NLDAS-2 / Stage IV is bias-corrected to gauge and PRISM climatology and disaggregated to hours with radar, satellite, reanalysis and GDAS data; so the hours before 2002 are disaggregated daily totals, not hourly observations, and from 2002 on they follow the radar analysis. All training years (1980-2000) lie in the first period and all test years (2005-2014) in the second, so the network learns the timing of rain within the day from a disaggregation and is scored on radar-based timing (against the hourly Stage IV files the pooled hourly correlation at lag 0 is 0.98 on storm days of the test years and 0.67 on storm days of 2000-2001; against the cached ERA5 hourly rain it is 0.41 before 2002 and 0.41 from 2002 on, median of the basins: ERA5 does not tell the two kinds of hours apart). AORC is an analysis made after the fact (about 10 days after the hour in operation, from the same summary, unverified), not rain that anyone could have read at midnight: in real time the same hours would come from Stage IV or MRMS radar (about 1 hour behind) or from satellite rain such as IMERG-Early (about 4 hours behind). One more caveat: the daily totals that anchor the hours cover a gauge day that does not end at local midnight (12 UTC), so the value given to an hour before midnight could have been scaled with information from the rain after it; the clock proof shows which hours are summed, not that every hour's value was made without later information. That question was open when this script was first run; it has been measured since. An independent review (results/review_aorc_rain_to_midnight.json) tested what that could do to the test years: on 78 days (936 basin-days) the AORC rain before local midnight does not depend on the Stage IV rain after it (coefficient -0.030 mm per mm, 95% interval -0.060 to -0.001), and with Stage IV, a real-time product (about one hour behind), in place of AORC on the issue day the three networks of seeds 0-2 that the review tested warn of 86 to 95 of the 171 onsets of those days against 92 with AORC (the rain table alone: 15), that is 92% to 104% of the AORC effect; a hindsight that the review could not exclude would cost those networks at most about 3 points of their 51% (16 of 313 hits); the other 440 onsets were not tested by the review; with all five networks, Stage IV in place of AORC on the issue day costs 22 of 316 hits on all 611 onsets (3.6 points; 5 hits, 0.8 points, with the level of AORC restored). The builder's own check (results/aorc_hindsight.json: 50 stormiest days, 600 basin-days) found a coefficient of +0.035 (-0.078 to +0.138), but its days hold only 1.1 mm of Stage IV rain in the 7 hours after midnight against 21.8 mm before, so its interval mostly reflects how little night rain it contains; the 28 days that the review added, chosen by onsets and by night storms, hold 11.8 mm. Stage IV in place of AORC on the issue day of all 611 onsets (results/stage4_realtime.json): 294 of 611 warned against 316 with AORC and 114 with the rain table alone, 89% of the AORC effect survives (95% interval 83% to 95%, drawing issue days); with the last hour of the issue day taken out, as the delay of Stage IV would, 276 are warned (80% of the effect) and with the level of AORC restored (Stage IV times 1.06) 311. That count is driven by heavy rain on the issue day more than by its exact amount: with the Stage IV rain of another onset day of the same basin in its place 286 onsets are warned, with the AORC rain of an ordinary day 36, with no rain 13; the mean absolute error of the forecast on the onset days, which does depend on the exact rain, is 4.64 mm/day with Stage IV, 4.62 with AORC and 5.64 with another onset's rain. E1b therefore measures what gauge- and radar-anchored rain up to midnight is worth if it were known as well as AORC knows it, not what a real-time service delivers.

Day alignment. The Daymet rain stamped day d correlates 0.54 with the AORC rain of the local day d, 0.74 with that of day d-1 and 0.04 with that of day d+1 (median of the 12 basins; daily_rain.check); the ERA5 rain of script 15 correlates 0.75 with the AORC rain of the same local day (0.24 with d-1, 0.12 with d+1). A Daymet day that ends in the morning (09:00 local time, readings 07:28 to 10:42) shares its hours with two local days, d-1 and d, and none with d+1: the correlations show that pattern, so the two series are aligned as described. Over the whole record the AORC daily rain is 0.96 times the Daymet rain in the median basin (ERA5: 0.85).

Clock of the controls (aorc_to_09 and aorc_utc_day). The same hourly AORC values as aorc_to_midnight, summed over other windows by the same code, and proved for all 12 basins and all 12418 days in the same way as in script 15: (1) every hour summed into day t starts at or after the start and ends at or before the end of its window, in absolute (UTC) time and on the clock of the window, and ends at or before the issue time of day t (local midnight at the end of day t, as a UTC time, and 24:00 by the wall clock); (2) the same daily rain by a second route, from the time-zone rules, and every hour lies in the same day in both routes; (3) the rain after the end of the window of 3 random days per basin, and of the first days of 23 and of 25 hours, was replaced by made-up values: no value up to that day changed (daily_rain.windows). The code for any window reproduces aorc_to_midnight exactly (asserted). aorc_to_09 is the wall-clock window from 09:00 of day t-1 to 09:00 of day t, the window of the rain table itself: results/day_windows.json (day_ends.daymet) measured it to end at 08:48 local standard time (basins 07:26 to 18:16, readings 07:28 to 10:42), rounded to 09:00; the code uses the wall clock like the main series, so in summer it ends one hour earlier in standard time, well inside the spread of the readings. Its last hour ends 15 hours before the issue time. aorc_utc_day is the UTC day of the date of day t: from 00:00 UTC of that date to 00:00 UTC of the next date, always 24 hours, 19:00 local standard time in the Eastern basins and 18:00 in Leaf River, by the wall clock between 18:00 and 20:00; its last hour ends 4 to 6 hours before the issue time, so the proof of nothing after the issue time holds with that margin. A rain product served by UTC day (IMERG at NASA POWER) or IMERG-Early with its delay of about 4 hours would have that UTC day at about the issue time; AORC summed over the UTC day stands in for it and is not it.

What the controls are for. Test minus control is the worth of what the test series holds and the control does not. aorc_to_09 is the same AORC product over the window of the table (as nearly as that window is known: it differs from basin to basin and between the readings), so it holds no hour that the table does not already cover, give or take the uncertainty of that window, and lstm_wqa minus lstm_wqa_to09 is the worth of the hours 09:00 to 24:00 of day t (value_of_hours_09_to_24), without the effect of having a second product; the Daymet rain stamped d correlates 0.91 with aorc_to_09 of the same day, against 0.54 with aorc_to_midnight (median of the basins; daily_rain.check_windows). aorc_utc_day holds the hours up to the end of the UTC day, so lstm_wqa minus lstm_wqa_utc is the worth of the evening hours beyond it (value_of_evening_hours_beyond_utc_day). The NLDAS day, as measured, is about 17:30 local standard time and, if stamped by the UTC day, 19:00; the NLDAS rain of the CAMELS files correlates 0.90 with aorc_utc_day of the same day, 0.79 with aorc_to_midnight and 0.77 with aorc_to_09 (the AORC window that NLDAS resembles most: aorc_utc_day).

The replaced table (wqa_rep = wqa_daymet_replaced). The input column that holds the Daymet rain (prcp) in every other set holds aorc_to_midnight here, in the same position: the set has the same inputs as lstm_wq with one column changed, so the same seed gives the same starting weights and the same sequence of training samples, and the difference to lstm_wq is the content of the rain column (the AORC rain of the wall-clock day t, which ends at the issue time, against the Daymet day that ends at about 09:00 and belongs to another product). The daily sequence the network reads still holds every hour the table plus the extra column holds - the hours before day t sit in the earlier days - except that the Daymet product itself is gone; the comparison with lstm_wqa (AORC as an extra column beside Daymet) shows what keeping the Daymet column adds. It addresses the second question of step 1b of the roadmap (whether the mis-stamped table itself costs skill) only in part: it changes the clock and the product together, and the same AORC rain over the table's own window in the place of the Daymet column (aorc_to_09 as the only rain column) was not run.

The checks (gain_rule). A gain in the median NSE is called clear when three things agree: every single seed with the new input is above every single seed of the model it is compared with (the comparison is made with the control, with the rain table alone, with NLDAS and with ERA5); the NSE is higher in most of the 12 basins; and the Wilcoxon signed-rank p (two-sided, over the basins) is below 0.05. The onsets warned are pooled over the basins, so no basin count or p exists for them: there only the seeds are compared (as in 10_rain_timing.py). The basins share storms, so p describes and does not prove. With one seed (a smoke test) no seed range can say anything.

AORC's hours before 2002 are disaggregated daily totals and all training years lie before 2002 (all test years after): a network trained on radar-era hours (from 2002 on) would need a training period of its own, which this split does not have; this was not tried. What the hours of a daily-total disaggregation can teach the network about the timing of rain within the day was not measured separately.

For the gauges whose flow day follows standard time in summer (results/day_windows.json), the wall-clock day ends one hour before their flow day, so one hour of rain is left out of the new input for them in summer; what that hour would add was not measured, and the flow-day check covers only part of one year.
